The central question is whether the memory layout of KV caches — specifically how key-value pairs from different sequence positions get allocated, evicted, and reused across heterogeneous attention layers — systematically distorts which tokens a model can reliably retrieve versus which it merely "sees" during a forward pass. In sliding-window layers, only a local context window is attended to, so those KV entries can be cached in short, contiguous blocks; but in full-attention layers interleaved throughout the architecture (as in Mistral, Gemma 2, or similar hybrids), the cache must suddenly reference the entire sequence history, meaning any fragmentation — gaps from evicted tokens, non-contiguous physical memory blocks, or misaligned page boundaries in paged attention systems like vLLM — creates irregular access patterns that don't affect perplexity uniformly across positions. The expert worry that beginners miss is the positional asymmetry of retrieval failure: fragmentation doesn't degrade all tokens equally; it tends to drop or corrupt KV entries at boundaries between local and global attention layers, which are precisely the positions where information must "hand off" between the two regimes — and because this failure is silent (the model still produces fluent output), standard benchmarks that measure generation quality won't catch it. A secondary concern is cache invalidation coupling: in a hybrid architecture, evicting a token's KV entry from a sliding-window layer to free memory can force recomputation in the next full-attention layer that needed that entry, creating cascading latency spikes that are hard to profile because they're triggered by specific sequence-length thresholds, not by load alone.

The most severe fragmentation damage occurs at local→global boundaries, where a full-attention layer must reconstruct a complete KV context from entries that the preceding sliding-window layers never fully populated. In Mistral 7B's original architecture, global attention layers appear roughly every 4th layer with a sliding window of 4096 tokens in the local layers; any token outside that 4096-token window was never written into the cache by the local layers, so when the global layer attempts to attend over the full sequence, it either recomputes those KV entries on-the-fly (expensive) or attends over a structurally incomplete cache (quietly wrong). The global→local direction is less catastrophic because the sliding-window layer simply ignores most of the cache by design — fragmentation in distant positions is irrelevant since the local attention mask already excludes them — though it does waste memory bandwidth fetching blocks that will be masked out. What makes local→global boundaries specifically treacherous in paged attention systems (vLLM's default block size is 16 tokens) is that eviction policies like LRU or frequency-based scoring optimize for sliding-window reuse patterns, meaning low-frequency early-sequence tokens — often the most semantically critical ones, like instruction preambles or document titles — are precisely the entries most likely to be evicted before a global layer needs them. Empirically, the Needle-in-a-Haystack failure mode in long-context evaluations (128k+ sequences) clusters disproportionately at positions corresponding to these eviction-vulnerable ranges, not uniformly across sequence length, which is the concrete signature of boundary-driven rather than capacity-driven retrieval failure.

A schedule-aware eviction policy would need to treat KV entries not as uniform cache lines but as typed resources tagged with which layer classes will consume them — concretely, a token at position p needs a "global-layer retention score" separate from its recency score, because its value to a full-attention layer at depth d+4 is independent of whether any sliding-window layer at d+1 through d+3 recently touched it. The minimum additional metadata current systems don't track is: (1) the next global attention layer index that will need this token's KV entry, (2) the token's attention sink probability — the empirical finding from StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) that initial tokens receive disproportionate attention mass regardless of content — and (3) a cross-layer access forecast, essentially a lightweight predictor of whether this token will receive above-threshold attention weight when the next global layer fires. Systems like vLLM and SGLang currently evict based purely on recency and block-level granularity (16–32 token pages), with no awareness of the serving model's layer topology at all — the eviction engine doesn't even receive the model config that would tell it a global layer is 2 layers away. A concrete implementation would integrate with the model's attention schedule manifest (the fixed, known pattern of local/global layer alternation) to set a protected retention window: any token within the current sequence that a global layer will attend to within the next k forward steps gets flagged non-evictable, with k tuned to prefill latency budgets. The harder unsolved problem is that attention sink membership and semantic salience (instruction tokens, named entities, coreference anchors) aren't statically knowable at cache-write time without running a forward pass — meaning a truly optimal policy requires either a cheap proxy model scoring tokens at ingestion, or retroactive promotion when attention weights are observed during the global layer's forward pass, which is after the damage of eviction may already be done.

The feedback loop is theoretically sound — after a global layer computes attention weights, you have a ranked list of which token positions received high attention mass, and you could immediately re-score those cache entries as high-priority before the next global layer fires k layers later — but the implementation hits a pipeline parallelism wall: in tensor-parallel or pipeline-parallel serving (the default for any model >13B parameters across multiple GPUs), attention weights are computed and discarded within a single pipeline stage, and the KV cache manager lives in a separate process or thread that never sees those weights. Concretely, in vLLM's architecture, the scheduler and cache engine operate asynchronously from the model executor; feeding attention weights back would require either a synchronous cross-process write on every global layer forward pass (serializing the pipeline) or a dedicated side-channel buffer that the executor writes to and the cache engine reads from between layer steps, neither of which exists today. The latency budget is brutally tight: in continuous batching at high throughput, the window between one global layer completing and the next eviction decision is often sub-millisecond, and any feedback mechanism that adds even 50–100μs of synchronization overhead measurably reduces tokens-per-second at batch sizes where KV memory pressure is actually a problem. A partial solution that avoids full synchronization is speculative retention: after the first global layer fires, asynchronously write the top-k attended positions (just their indices, not the weights) to a ring buffer, and have the eviction policy check that buffer opportunistically rather than blocking on it — meaning some evictions still happen before the feedback arrives, but the policy improves over the sequence's lifetime. The deeper architectural constraint is that this feedback loop implicitly requires the cache manager to reason about future layer behavior, which conflicts with the stateless, request-agnostic design philosophy of current serving systems like SGLang and vLLM, where the cache engine is deliberately kept ignorant of model internals to support serving arbitrary model architectures without model-specific engineering.

The staleness question has a sharp empirical answer: attention sink positions (typically tokens 0–4) remain stable across all global layers, but semantic retrieval heads — the heads actually responsible for fetching specific facts — shift their top-k targets substantially as depth increases. Work from the InfLLM and LongBench analysis literature shows that early global layers attend broadly over structural positions (sentence boundaries, special tokens, syntactic anchors) while late global layers concentrate weight on semantically relevant tokens specific to the current query, meaning a top-k set captured at the first global layer has maybe 40–60% overlap with the top-k at the final global layer for retrieval-heavy tasks. This drift is faster in longer sequences: at 32k tokens the top-k set is relatively stable across layers because the retrieval target is a small fraction of total sequence length, but at 128k+ tokens, Retrieval head analyses (Fu et al., "Data Engineering for Scaling Language Models," 2024; and the H2O paper's follow-up ablations) suggest per-head top-k overlap between first and last global layer drops toward 30–40%, because the model is doing progressively more refined localization as depth increases. The practical implication for speculative retention is that it correctly protects attention sinks (high ROI, stable) but becomes unreliable for the semantically salient tokens that are actually the hard retrieval targets — precisely the entries most likely to be evicted under memory pressure and most damaging to lose. A further complication is head heterogeneity within a single global layer: even at the same layer, different attention heads attend to entirely different position sets (retrieval heads vs. induction heads vs. positional heads), so a single per-layer top-k index set conflates fundamentally different functional roles, and an eviction policy that doesn't distinguish head types will over-protect induction-head targets that are cheap to recompute and under-protect retrieval-head targets that are not.

Konkretely, a classifier needs only three per-head statistics computed from the attention weight matrix during the forward pass: (1) the effective attention span (mean attended position distance from current token), (2) the attendance sparsity (entropy or top-1 weight concentration), and (3) whether the top-attended positions cluster at fixed offsets (induction signature) versus scattered semantic positions (retrieval signature) — these three numbers fit in under 100 bytes per head and can be computed as a side-effect of the softmax that's already happening. The feasibility of online classification is supported by the Retrieval Head paper (Wu et al., 2024), which showed that retrieval heads are largely consistent across inputs for a given model, meaning a brief calibration pass over 50–100 representative sequences can pre-classify heads offline, reducing the online inference cost to a simple lookup table indexed by (layer, head) — no runtime classification needed at all during serving. The harder problem is that head function isn't perfectly static: retrieval heads can behave like induction heads on repetitive inputs, and vice versa on highly novel sequences, so a static lookup table will misclassify maybe 10–15% of head-step combinations under distribution shift, which is tolerable for eviction policy purposes but not for anything requiring hard guarantees. A practical implementation would use the offline calibration table as the default, with a lightweight online override triggered only when a head's current attention entropy deviates more than a threshold from its calibrated baseline — adding perhaps 5–10 microseconds per global layer per request, well within the latency budget established in the previous turn's analysis.

In a continuous batching regime with heterogeneous requests, the fundamental problem is that KV cache pages are shared at the block level (16–32 tokens in vLLM), not the request level, meaning a single physical page may be referenced by a code-completion request and a long-document retrieval request simultaneously — and the eviction protection decision for that page cannot be simultaneously optimized for both requests' head classification profiles. Per-request head classification becomes necessary only if the within-batch variance in retrieval head behavior exceeds the eviction policy's error tolerance; empirically, code and natural language requests show the largest divergence, with retrieval heads in code-focused layers attending heavily to identifier positions while the same heads on prose inputs scatter across semantic anchors, suggesting batches mixing these two domains will have ~20–30% head classification disagreement on the pages they share. The practical resolution is request-type clustering at the scheduler level — SGLang's radix attention already implicitly does something like this by routing requests with common prefixes to shared cache blocks, and extending that logic to route by inferred task type (classification, retrieval, generation) would keep head-behavior-similar requests on the same physical pages, reducing cross-request eviction policy conflict without per-request runtime classification. The cost isolation problem in continuous batching is more subtle: per-request classification overhead can't be amortized across the batch the way compute is, because each request's attention entropy statistics are private to its KV entries — the cheapest architecture is a shadow statistics buffer per request that accumulates head entropy observations across global layers and is evaluated asynchronously by a cache management thread, adding memory overhead of roughly (num_heads × num_global_layers × 3 floats) per active request, which at 32 heads and 8 global layers is under 3KB per request and negligible against KV cache footprints in the tens of gigabytes. The unresolved tension is that continuous batching's efficiency comes precisely from treating all requests as fungible consumers of shared resources, and any system that needs per-request metadata to make eviction decisions is swimming against that architectural current — the more heterogeneous the workload, the more the efficiency gains of batching are eroded by the overhead of maintaining request-private cache management state.

The tradeoff has a principled formulation: define a clustering efficiency loss as the fractional reduction in mean batch size from type-constrained scheduling, and a retrieval fidelity gain as the reduction in eviction-driven retrieval failures weighted by their downstream task impact — the system should cluster only when the fidelity gain in expected task reward exceeds the throughput cost in tokens-per-second. Concretely, batching efficiency degrades nonlinearly with clustering stringency: if your workload is 60% retrieval, 30% code, 10% classification, forcing same-type batches reduces effective batch size by roughly the inverse of the dominant type's frequency squared under Poisson arrival assumptions, meaning throughput drops ~20–25% at that mix before you've gained anything on fidelity — a cost that's only recoverable if retrieval failures were actually occurring at a rate that affected quality metrics. The empirical crossover point appears around workload entropy of ~0.7–0.8 bits (on a 0-to-log2(N) scale across N task types): below that, the workload is dominated by one or two types and clustering is nearly free; above it, the batch fragmentation cost dominates and a better strategy is to accept classification noise and compensate with a more conservative global eviction threshold rather than clustering at all. A more tractable intermediate approach — suggested by the Sarathi-Serve paper's chunked prefill analysis — is to cluster only the prefill phase, where KV pages are being written and head classification is being established, while allowing heterogeneous mixing during the decode phase where eviction decisions are actually made; this captures most of the fidelity benefit while recovering batching efficiency during the computationally dominant decode stage. The deeper quantitative difficulty is that retrieval fidelity loss from eviction is not directly observable in production without ground-truth answers to compare against, so the "gain" side of the tradeoff must be estimated from proxy signals like attention reconstruction error or cache miss rates — making the optimization effectively a bandit problem where you're trading a measurable throughput cost against a latent quality benefit you can only noisily observe.
